cards.title: Treat Every Ad as a Salesman Held to Sales Standards
cards.summary: Judge advertising by whether it would help a real salesperson close a sale, not by whether it entertains or wins applause.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or briefing any ecommerce ad creative (Meta, TikTok, Google, email), or arbitrating disagreements about a headline, slogan or image in a campaign.
steps: Before approving any ad, ask the two diagnostic questions: 'Would this help a salesperson sell the goods?' and 'Would it help me sell them if I met the buyer in person?' If the answer is no for a functional reason, cut the element.

Reframe the ad's job: it is multiplied salesmanship addressing thousands, not a slogan or brand-awareness vehicle. Every dollar spent is a mistake multiplied across all your trade, so be more exacting than you would with a single sales rep.

Strip performative elements — clever conceits, literary style, attention-grabbing gimmicks — because any apparent attempt to sell creates resistance. People resent feeling over-influenced and suspect the pitch is not on merit.
Write to one typical individual buyer, not to 'people in the mass'; a blurred mass view produces generic copy that converts poorly.

Consider having a real sales conversation or watching customer support transcripts before writing — Hopkins notes some of the ablest ad men spent weeks selling door to door to learn which arguments landed.
If an element survives the salesperson test but is there for pride or aesthetics, keep it knowingly and record its cost, rather than assuming it is neutral.
caveats: Hopkins's rule is a directional filter, not a way to skip testing; the salesperson test alone does not substitute for keyed return data.
This is Hopkins's strong opinion, not an established law; brand-building and top-of-funnel creative can have value that direct-response metrics do not capture.

cards.title: Write the Headline to Hail Only the Interested Segment
cards.summary: A headline's job is to pick out the specific subset of readers who can be interested in the product and address them directly.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing headlines for an ecommerce ad, PDP hero, email subject line or landing page, where you must attract the right buyer rather than maximize raw clicks.
steps: Identify the narrow segment your product actually serves and the reason they would care (e.g. corsets → women; cigars → smokers). Explicitly discard irrelevant audiences before writing.
Write the headline as a direct hail to that segment — Hopkins's 'Hey there, Bill Jones' in a crowd — so the right reader instantly knows the ad is for them.
Avoid blind or clever headlines even if they pull many more readers; the extra readers are mostly people with no use for your offer and the actual prospects may never realize the ad refers to them.

Test by keyed returns: Hopkins reports that running an identical ad with different headlines can multiply returns five to ten times, and he kept keyed returns on nearly 2,000 headlines for a single product.

Because one product has many uses (beauty, disease prevention, cleanliness), run a variety of ads so each appeal reaches its own audience; accept that a weaker appeal may still be profitable even at half the returns of the best one.
Compare each headline against actual cost per customer or per dollar of sale, not volume of clicks, before deciding which appeal is dominant and how to allocate ads.
caveats: The five-to-ten-times multiplier is Hopkins's historical mail-order observation, not a benchmark for your channel; verify with your own keyed tests.
Headline appeal differs per product line; do not copy another brand's winning headline style as a universal rule.

cards.title: Replace Superlatives With Specific, Verifiable Claims
cards.summary: General claims and superlatives are discounted by readers; a precise number or process earns full weight.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ad copy, offer claims or comparison copy where you need a claim to be believed rather than dismissed as hype.
steps: Audit your copy for platitudes and superlatives — 'best in the world', 'lowest price in existence', 'pure', 'quality'. These claim only the expected and suggest careless truth, leading readers to discount everything you say.
Convert each into a specific, checkable fact: instead of 'more light' say 'three and one-third times the light'; instead of 'prices reduced' say 'prices reduced 25 percent'.

For pricing claims, a bold specific disclosure can outperform a superlative: a clothing advertiser replaced 'Lowest prices in America' with 'Our net profit is 3 percent' and business increased sensationally; likewise a car maker stated 'Our profit is 9 percent' and itemized $735 of hidden costs on a $1,500 car.

Turn ordinary brewing or manufacturing steps into specific story facts, as a brewer did — a plate-glass cooling room, 1,018 yeast experiments, water drawn from 4,000 feet — because these are mere essentials in the industry that no one has bothered to tell buyers.
Quantify tests and comparisons: '78-second shave', 'softens the beard in one minute', '130 formulas tested'. Such statements imply you actually tested and compared.
Use exact scope instead of elastic claims: 'Used by the peoples of 52 nations' rather than 'Used the world over'.
Check any number you put in copy is true and defensible; Hopkins treats a specific claim as either truth or a lie, and buyers treat it accordingly.
caveats: Do not invent figures, tests or percentages you cannot substantiate — a specific claim is a claim of fact.
Specificity only works once; rivals copied the '52 nations' phrasing, so periodically refresh the fact you lead with.

cards.title: Lead With Service, Not a Buy Request
cards.summary: Offers that give the buyer something (trial, sample, useful information, risk-free approval) outsell ads that simply ask for the order.
cards.use_when: Designing an offer or acquisition creative for a hard-to-sell product, cold audience or high-consideration purchase where a direct 'buy now' ask is underperforming.
steps: Rewrite the ad around the buyer's side of the service — advantages to users, information they want — rather than the brand's interests. The self-interested appeal ('Buy my brand, give me the trade') is unpopular.
Consider offers that let the buyer prove the claim at no cost or risk: a sample, approval, trial period, or the first package paid for by the maker rather than given away.

Case evidence Hopkins cites: an electric sewing-machine motor maker stopped soliciting a purchase and offered a one-week in-home trial with a demonstrator; about nine in ten trials led to sales. Do not treat that rate as a forecast for your product, but the trial mechanism is the transferable idea.

Distinguish paid trials from freebies: both advertisers offered a full-size package to poorer-class buyers, but the one whose coupon let the buyer get a package the maker paid retail for succeeded, while the one who gave it free failed and lost trade — a free 15-cent package cheapened the product.

Make sampling opt-in rather than shoved at people: a housewife handed an unwanted sample pays it no respect; one who requests a sample after reading the story arrives knowing and expecting the claimed qualities.
For neighborhood or marketplace channels, mimic the brush-canvasser tactic: open by offering a choice of free samples so the prospect engages and reciprocates, rather than asking for an order first.
caveats: Approval and sample offers rely on people being honest; Hopkins reports losses are very small, but this is his mail-order-era experience, not a modern guarantee.
Repeated free sampling can train buyers to expect free product, making later purchase feel like a downgrade.
Physical sample programs have fulfillment and fraud costs that must be measured against incremental orders.

cards.title: Tell the Full Story in One Ad — No Serials
cards.summary: Once you have a reader's attention, present every important claim in that single ad; do not split arguments across a series.
cards.use_when: Structuring ad copy, PDP or landing page content where you must decide how much of the argument to include and whether to serialise messaging across multiple touchpoints.
steps: Inventory your appealing claims by testing headline variants and comparing results; keep an accumulated list of claims that have proven to pull.
Put every claim on that list into each ad thereafter, because one fact appeals to one reader and another to another; omitting any one loses the percentage that fact would have convinced.
Refuse the serial-ad approach — 'continued in the next issue' ads rarely connect, and a person who has read and decided once is unlikely to reread, just as no one rereads a news item.

Apply the rule-of-thumb: a complete story may be one sentence for a low-consideration product like chewing gum, but it must still be reasonably complete; for high-consideration purchases it may run to columns — a car buyer read full columns and books before choosing.

Do not waste space addressing existing customers; they already read and decided and will not read your ads. Assume every reader is an unconverted prospect and write for them. You may advertise that their current product is poison and they would never see it.

Accept monotony for repeat readers: a complete story is always the same, and single mail-order ads have run year after year without diminishing returns because returns come from new readers, not repeat ones.
Note that brief ads are rarely keyed or traced; ignore untraced examples of 'short is better' and be guided by your own traced results.
caveats: The 'more you tell, the more you sell' maxim held in tested mail order; in modern short-form video and skippable ad units the format itself constrains copy length, so test the full-story principle within the format's limits.
Complete story does not mean padding; every line must carry an argument that has proven its pulling power.

cards.title: Use Mail-Order Discipline as the Benchmark for All Ads
cards.summary: Ads that sell goods by direct response are the severest test of copy and a model for economy of space, pictures and words.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your ecommerce ad creative is wasting budget on decoration, big type or design quirks, or when you lack any keyed results to judge an ad by.
steps: Study long-running, clearly profitable direct-response ads and note the concrete patterns Hopkins identifies: small type (proved that larger type does not pay — doubling type doubles space while adding no added sales), no waste space or borders, no boasting, no palaver, no attempt to amuse.

Note their pictures: always to the point and earning their space, sized by their selling importance — a dress picture may take much space, minor items get small space. Pictures in untraced advertising may only produce whims.

Take the incubator case as a cautionary example, not a law: an advertiser added a silhouette row of chickens, increasing space 50 percent, and cost per reply rose exactly 50 percent with not one added sale, because incubator buyers were practical people looking for offers, not pictures.

Treat size as proportional only if utilized: a twice-larger ad brings about twice the returns and a four-times-larger ad about four times, but only when the larger space is used as well as the small — setting half-page copy in a page space doubles cost per return.

Key and trace your own ads wherever possible. In mail order, cost per reply and cost per dollar of sale are immediate and exact; in non-direct lines, compare towns, methods or cost of sales to get comparable data.
Base final conclusions on cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale, not raw reply volume — one ad may bring many worthless replies, another fewer valid ones.
caveats: Hopkins's examples (incubators, cycle ads) are era-specific; extract the principle of traced economy, not the specific formats.
Deliberately attractive design can have brand value; Hopkins allows this but insists you know and record what it costs in returns.
Some direct-response ads are ugly and crowded by design choice, not necessity; copy the tested pattern, not the ugliness.

cards.title: Key and Trace Ads to Replace Guesswork With Fixed Principles
cards.summary: Repeated keyed tests, watched at cost-per-reply and cost-per-sale, convert advertising from gambling into a science with reusable laws.
cards.use_when: Setting up an experiment cadence for ecommerce ad creative, PDP tests, headline tests or offer tests, and deciding what metric to judge them on.
steps: Use a traceable mechanism — a coupon code, dedicated URL, unique reply mechanism — to measure the action each ad engenders, then compare one ad, headline, argument, size or picture against another.
Record every result with the headline and creative that produced it, so you accumulate a database of what pays rather than an anecdote.

Note the illustrative spread Hopkins gives: one five-dollar article's replies cost 85 cents, another submitted ad cost $14.20 per reply, and another brought replies at an average of 41 cents — on 250,000 replies a year the difference is enormous. Compare your figures to your own best, not to these.
Judge variations at the end of the chain — cost per customer or cost per dollar of sale — because cheap replies can be worthless ones.
When a method invariably proves best, promote it to a fixed principle and stop retesting it for that line; then reserve experimentation for the variable factors of people and products.
Where direct returns are impossible, run town-by-town, region-by-region or channel-by-channel comparisons measured by cost of sales to get an equivalent signal.
Expect your own judgment to be wrong often: Hopkins says one quickly loses conceit by learning how often judgment errs, 'often nine times in ten', which is why untraced preference is not evidence.
caveats: Small tests produce noisy results; Hopkins's agency compared thousands of ads and hundreds of lines to reach dependable conclusions.
Principles derived from one line may apply only to analogous undertakings; treat line-specific findings as hypotheses until tested in yours.

cards.title: Apply Fixed Psychological Levers That Still Drive Buying
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price-as-quality signals, personal ownership and class-restricted offers can be used deliberately to lift response.
cards.use_when: Designing ad angles, offer framing or PDP persuasion elements for an ecommerce product, notably when the product's real qualities are similar to competitors'.
steps: Use curiosity as a headline and angle device: Puffed Wheat and Puffed Rice succeeded largely on claims like 'grains puffed to 8 times the normal size' and '125 million steam explosions in every kernel' after failing without that framing.

Do not sell cheapness — sell the feeling the buyer can afford the best; treating buyers as unable to afford quality ('cheapness' appeals) causes resentment, whereas a department store's $1,000 Easter hat drew crowds of women who came to see it.

Use price and premium numbers as quality signals when relevant: a National Gallery painting was ignored until the catalog noted it cost $750,000, after which people returned to surround it. Stating a large sum paid for a formula (e.g. $100,000) won respect where a vague claim did not.

Prefer to send goods with no money down and collect later, rather than money-back guarantees: both refund and pay-later offers tested, and pay-in-a-week-if-you-like-them proved many times more impressive than refund promises.

Make ownership personal: offering to put the buyer's name in gilt on each book, with no other meaningful change, sold hundreds of thousands of books; a leather-covered book with the man's name on it, waiting to be requested, got nearly all recipients to respond and supply qualifying information.
Restrict offers to a named class (war veterans, lodge or sect members, executives), because those entitled to an advantage will go far not to lose it.

Handle substitution with an invitation rather than a warning: 'Look out for substitutes' failed as a selfish appeal, while 'Try our rivals too' — inviting comparison — corrected the situation and made buyers insist on the conspicuously superior brand.
caveats: These are Hopkins's tested mail-order examples; measure each lever in your own audience rather than assuming the same magnitude.
Fabricating a paid-price figure that is not true is a false claim; the $100,000 formula statement was presented as fact.
Name-personalisation and restricted offers can raise cost and complexity per order; check margin impact.

cards.title: Use the Questionable Persona or Trusted Neighbour as the Seller
cards.summary: Attributing the offer to a credible human — a photographed, named dealer or a woman customers identify with — can beat an impersonal business offer.
cards.use_when: Building the 'from' identity for ecommerce ads, email, WhatsApp or DMs, especially for credit, instalment or higher-risk categories where trust is the barrier.
steps: Choose whether to speak as a company or as a named individual. Hopkins describes two side-by-side women's clothing instalment concerns: one made a bare business offer to poorer girls and the other put a motherly, dignified woman in charge, used her name on all ads and letters, and wrote like a friend — the impersonal rival had to quit.
Have the named persona sign all communications in their own voice and use their picture, so ads and correspondence reinforce the same trusted identity.

Position the persona's motivation as service to the buyer's situation — Hopkins's example: she knew what it meant for a girl not to dress her best and had long wanted to supply good clothes with all season to pay.

For credit or delayed-payment offers, use a warm recommendation to extend credit rather than a bare credit offer, which can seem like a reflection: tell the customer that a known, paying customer recommended her and that a credit account is open, no advance payment, order any time.

Adapt the neighbour-warrant tactic: a far-away guarantee is unremarkable, but a dealer who signs a written warrant to refund on request, in the buyer's own neighbourhood, made a fortune for one concern and has proved effective whenever tried.
Extend the same logic to marketplace or reseller trust signals: attribute the guarantee to a local, named party rather than an anonymous brand.
caveats: The persona must be real or clearly representational to the customer; inventing fake testimonials would be deceptive.
These are historical mail-order cases; the trust mechanism transfers but the specific credit-granting model may not fit every category.
Using a persona's photo and name across ads is a commitment; inconsistency between the persona and actual support weakens the effect.

cards.title: Budget Ads Around Proven Claims, Not Around the Seller's Taste
cards.summary: The appeals you personally prefer rarely perform best, because you do not know enough people to average out their desires.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ad angles and headlines to scale in an ecommerce campaign, especially when your personal favourite is underperforming and a plain or surprising angle is winning.
steps: Assume your taste is not representative: Hopkins states outright that the appeals we like best will rarely prove best, so preference is not a reason to scale an ad.

Learn the dominant appeal on each line by comparison. For a soap, 'Keep Clean' and 'No animal fat' might attract few readers, 'It floats' might interest more, while a beauty or complexion headline might pull many times as many — you only know by testing.

Do not assume technical features persuade: an automobile headline about a good universal joint may fall flat because few buyers think about universal joints, while 'The Sportiest of Sport Bodies' may out-pull it fifty to one.
Let each tested appeal have its share of spend: an appeal that brings half the returns of the best can still be profitable, and you skip no paying field.

Run multiple distinct ads for overlapping audiences — Hopkins notes using twenty separate ads across twenty magazines because circulation overlaps and different percentages of people respond to different approaches.
Allocate spend across appeals in proportion to proven pulling power, learned through experiment, not through internal debate.
caveats: The 50-to-1 and five-to-ten-times figures are Hopkins's keyed mail-order examples; use them as illustrations of variance, not as expected effects.
Multiple ads raise production cost and testing complexity; protect enough budget per variant to reach a readable result.

cards.title: Judge Pictures by Their Selling Cost, Not Their Charm
cards.summary: Pictures consume one-third to one-half of many campaign budgets, so each must earn its space through tested selling power.
cards.use_when: Approving or cutting images in ecommerce ad creative, PDP galleries or landing pages when deciding whether an image justifies its place and cost.
steps: Estimate the share of spend tied to visuals: Hopkins says from one-third to one-half of an advertising campaign is often staked on the power of the pictures, in space cost as well as production cost.
Do not use a picture merely because it is interesting, attention-getting or decorative; treat that as waste unless a test proves it pays.

Score each image on what it sells: in tested direct-response ads pictures are always to the point and act as salesmen in themselves, and their size is gauged by selling importance — a dress one is selling may occupy much space, minor items less.

Test image additions against cost per reply or cost per sale. The incubator advertiser added a row of silhouette chickens, increased space 50 percent, and his cost per reply rose exactly 50 percent with no added sales.

Infer from the incubator result that picture value is audience- and category-dependent: those buyers were practical people seeking attractive offers, not imagery. Do not generalise the result to image-driven categories such as apparel.
Compare the same ad with and without the picture before rolling a visual treatment out at scale.
caveats: The 50 percent cost increase is a single case study, not a rule; some ecommerce categories legitimately sell on imagery.
Pictures in untraced general advertising may teach little and result in whims, per Hopkins — so untested visual conventions are weak evidence.
This is Hopkins's opinion from mail-order testing; modern feed advertising may show different image dynamics that require your own tests.

cards.title: Interview and Sell to Buyers Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: Direct contact with prospective customers reveals the arguments and approaches that actually land, replacing expensive guesswork.
cards.use_when: Preparing copy for a product launch or a stalled ecommerce campaign where you have no reliable data on what buyers respond to.
steps: Talk to prospective buyers directly before planning the ad. Hopkins notes it was customary to interview hundreds of possible customers, and one of the ablest ad men spent weeks on a single article selling from house to house.
Use those conversations to learn what buyers want and which factors do not appeal, testing different forms of argument and approach as you go.
Alternatively send questionnaires to learn buyers' attitudes, or study support chats and reviews for the same signal-capture purpose.

Recognise the maker's blind spot: the maker knows manufacturing and the dealer side, but that very knowledge leads him astray about customers because his interests are not their interests — so treat internal assumptions as suspect.
Have the copywriter place themselves in the buyer's position to the exclusion of other perspectives; Hopkins calls this one of the most important determinants of success.
Use findings to build the claim list and headline variants for keyed testing rather than launching a fully untested campaign.
caveats: No method for determining purchasing preferences was found in the source text; the reliability of questionnaire responses is not established here.
Small interview samples may not represent your broader market; validate chat and interview insights with keyed tests before committing spend.

cards.title: Use Test Campaigns to Set Spend Before Scaling
cards.summary: Small, keyed and traced tests establish which method pays before a full campaign commits ad budget.
cards.use_when: Planning the launch sequence and media budget for a new ecommerce product, market or creative concept before scaling spend.
steps: Run the ad in a limited, keyed test first and read the results at cost per reply and cost per dollar of sale before scaling to full campaign spend.
Where direct response is not measurable, run matched town or region tests measuring cost of sales, and compare scores of methods across those cells.
Record every variation compared — headline, setting, size, argument, picture — so the test yields reusable principles, not just a go/no-go.
Expect frequent wrong readings of your own judgment; Hopkins says one learns how often judgment errs, often nine times in ten, which is why untested scale-up is dangerous.

When you find an ad that pays, protect it: Hopkins cites Mr. Mead of the Mead Cycle Company saying he would not change a single word for $10,000, because the ads you see are the final results of many years of comparisons.
Refresh only when a tested replacement beats the incumbent; long-running winning creative should not be changed for novelty.
caveats: Small market tests may not generalise to national audiences or other channels; results are directional.
The mechanics of keyed coupons and traced mail-order ads are era-specific; translate the testing principle into trackable links, codes and post-purchase attribution appropriate to your stack.
Verify current platform testing and attribution interfaces before relying on any particular measurement setup.

cards.title: Let Data Decide When Craft and Storytelling Pay
cards.summary: Every departure from tested direct-response economy has a measurable price; keep it only if you knowingly accept that cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in brand-style or design-led ecommerce creative versus plain, response-driven creative, and when defending or cutting costly creative elements.
steps: Separate the two reasons a general ad departs from winning direct-response form: the advertiser does not know what the direct-response advertiser knows (advertising blindly), or he deliberately sacrifices a percentage of returns to gratify a desire.
For each costly choice — fine design, big type, entertainment value, untested image — name what it is for and estimate the return loss through a keyed comparison.

Test deviations one at a time so the cost of each extravagance can be attributed: Hopkins asserts every departure from the principles adds to selling cost and that the nearer you get to proved direct-response copy the more customers you get for the money.
Do it if you can afford it, but know the price: Hopkins compares deliberate aesthetic sacrifice to fine offices and buildings — justifiable for pride, but only if you know what you are paying.
When returns fall short, return to a proven model ad and eliminate the identified waste rather than adding more ornament.
Distinguish personal pride in the creative from the reader's response; Hopkins notes some advertisers fall into trying to be performers and seek applause instead of sales.
caveats: This is Hopkins's strongly stated position, tied to direct-response measurement; brand-equity effects are difficult to attribute and may justify intentional deviation where tests cannot capture their value.
The 'always closer to mail-order copy means more customers' claim is a generalisation from tested mail-order lines, not a universal law for every category.
